points.description: Shows zero steady-state error: at steady state all derivatives vanish, including the integrator state, so ξ̇ = r − θ = 0, hence θ = r exactly, independent of a, b and c (ξ just settles at the value giving the needed constant control). Should note the requirement that the closed loop is stable so a steady state is reached. Merely asserting 'integral action removes error' without the ξ̇ = 0 ⇒ θ = r argument earns no marks.

levels.says: States that integral action gives zero error or that ξ̇ = 0 at steady state, but does not clearly conclude θ = r independent of b and c (or gives only a calculation for the specific values).

points.description: Names one valid practical failure mode of integral action AND gives its matching standard remedy. Acceptable pairs: integrator windup with anti-windup (clamping/conditional integration/back-calculation); reduced stability margin/phase lag with lowering KI, placing the integral pole slower than dominant poles, or adding derivative/feedforward; integration of sensor bias with calibration or leaky integrator. A failure mode with no remedy or a mismatched remedy earns at most half.

levels.says: Names a valid failure mode but gives no remedy or an incorrect/mismatched remedy.

rubric.notes: Full marks: the ξ̇ = r − θ = 0 ⇒ θ = r argument independent of b, c (with stability caveat), plus one valid failure mode with its remedy. Half marks for each point if only partly given as described. No marks for vague statements without the steady-state argument or a failure mode.
rubric.answer_key: At steady state all derivatives are zero, including the integrator state ξ̇ = r − θ = 0, so θ = r regardless of a, b, c (ξss = (c + b k1) r/(b KI) adjusts to supply the needed constant control; requires stability and b ≠ 0). Failure mode: integrator windup when the actuator saturates; remedy: anti-windup (conditional integration/clamping or back-calculation).
